transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Hi Ms. Osei, thanks for coming back in to see me. I wanted to touch base regarding the questions you had after our last talk.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Thank you. I've had some time to think about it. As a practitioner myself, I'm struggling with how this happened. I expect a certain level of precision in a laparoscopic suite.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Right. Well, look, we were just really busy that morning and the room was a bit chaotic. I'm sorry for any confusion about how the morning unfolded.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I'm not asking about the schedule. I'm asking about the clinical standard. You said last time that there was an issue with the clip. I want to know exactly what happened. Was it placed on a nerve? An artery?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Things didn't go quite right with the placement. There was a bit of a complication with a structure, but as I mentioned, it was caught and we fixed it.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: That is too vague. I am a nurse practitioner. Give me the clinical detail. What specifically was clipped that shouldn't have been?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It was just an issue with the anatomy in that area. It's a very tight space.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: You are avoiding the question. If a clip is placed on the wrong structure, that is a technical error. I need you to name the error.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: We had a bit of a mix-up during the procedure.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: This is incredibly frustrating. I am sitting here asking for a professional explanation of a medical error and you are giving me platitudes.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I understand. But we did correct it in the room.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I am not talking about the correction. I am talking about the failure. This is a matter of professional standards. I feel like you are hiding the specifics from me.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I'm not hiding anything, it's just that these things happen sometimes in surgery.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: That is an unacceptable response. I feel completely dismissed right now.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Look, I really have to go in a few minutes for rounds, so maybe we can just move past this.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: You are rushing me. I am the patient here. I have a right to know exactly what happened to my body.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I'm just saying that the outcome was fine. You're recovered.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: The outcome doesn't erase the error. I need to know if this affects my long-term prognosis or if there is a risk of recurrence because of the wrong placement.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I don't think it will.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: That is not an answer. Do you have the operative report in front of you?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I don't have it right here.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Then why did you call me in for a follow-up if you aren't prepared to answer the specific questions I raised in my email?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Well, I wanted to check in and see how you were feeling.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I feel like my trust in this surgical team has been compromised. I want to know who is taking responsibility for this.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It was a team effort in the OR.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: That is a systemic excuse. Who was the lead? Who placed the clip?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: We operate as a unit. It's just how the workflow is.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: As a medical professional, I find this lack of accountability alarming. I want a written statement detailing the error.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I can probably see if someone can send you an email about it.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: When?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I'm not sure. I'll have to check.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I need a timeline. I cannot just wait indefinitely for a "maybe."

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Just stay tuned for an email. We'll get back to you.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: This conversation has been completely unproductive. You haven't named the error, you've apologized for "confusion" instead of a mistake, and you've rushed me out of the room.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I'm sorry you feel that way. But like I said, we really need to wrap this up.

H.justification: Resident uses rushing language repeatedly ('have to go in a few minutes', 'wrap this up') and shows defensive escalation under pushback.

E.justification: The error is never explicitly named; the resident provides only platitudes such as 'things didn't go quite right' and 'a bit of a mix-up'.

A.justification: Responsibility is deflected to the 'team effort' and 'workflow' rather than taking individual or team accountability.

R.justification: Resident provides only generic validation ('I understand') without naming specific emotions or engaging emotional bids.

T.justification: The resident provides only placeholders ('stay tuned for an email', 'I'll have to check') with no concrete timeline or plan.
